query: Which material can be used for Temperature-dependent plastic deformation behaviors, and why?

generation.hypothesis: In an as-fabricated equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy, increasing the temperature will shift the dominant plastic deformation mechanism from dislocation slip and deformation twinning at lower temperatures to a regime where thermally activated processes (including slip coupled with partial recrystallization) prevail, resulting in lower yield strength and altered strain hardening behavior.
generation.material_initial_state: As-fabricated equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA with a face-centered cubic (FCC) structure and an inherent dislocation network (as produced, for example, via selective laser melting).
generation.intervention: Apply controlled mechanical deformation (tensile or compressive loading) while systematically varying the test temperature from room temperature up to temperatures above 700°C.
generation.conditions: Experiments conducted under a controlled temperature environment with in situ mechanical testing and microstructural characterization (e.g., using advanced electron microscopy and/or X-ray diffraction) to monitor evolving deformation mechanisms.
generation.structural_mediator: Temperature-induced modification of dislocation dynamics and local ordering transitions, specifically the activation of partial recrystallization at elevated temperatures.
generation.mechanism: At lower temperatures (e.g., 25°C to 600°C), plasticity is primarily accommodated by dislocation slip and twinning, leading to high yield strength and strain hardening. As temperature increases (≥700°C), thermally activated processes facilitate partial recrystallization, reducing the obstacles to dislocation motion and thereby lowering yield strength and changing strain hardening behavior.
generation.predicted_outcome: A measurable transition in the deformation mechanisms as temperature increases; specifically, a decrease in yield strength and a shift from twinning-dominated plasticity to slip accompanied by partial recrystallization.
generation.baseline: Room temperature behavior where plastic deformation is dominated by slip and twinning without significant recrystallization, leading to higher yield strength.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to the as-fabricated state of the alloy; however, if the material undergoes extensive microstructural evolution beyond annealing (e.g., grain growth or phase transformation into other structures), the observed behavior might fall outside the predicted regime.
generation.uncertainty: Precise transition temperatures and quantitative changes in mechanical properties are uncertain until validated by an integrated experimental and simulation approach; the interplay between dislocation processes and recrystallization requires further elucidation.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct in situ tensile or compressive tests on SLM-built equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA samples across a temperature range from 25°C to above 700°C. Utilize advanced electron microscopy and/or X-ray diffraction to observe microstructural changes (e.g., dislocation density, twinning vs. recrystallization events).
measurements: Yield strength and strain rate sensitivity
Occurrence and extent of deformation twinning and partial recrystallization
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If increasing temperature does not lead to a significant shift from twinning-dominated plasticity to slip with partial recrystallization, or if yield strength and strain hardening behavior remain invariant with temperature changes, then the hypothesis is falsified.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) are defined as equimolar or nonequimolar single- and multiphase solid solutions, depending on the number and type of principal/secondary metallic elements with the configurational entropy greater than 1.61 R , (where R is the gas constant) ( [1] , [2] ). The minimization of the Gibbs free energy by increasing the configurational entropy results in the formation of a single- or multiphase solid solution, such as body-centered cubic (BCC) ( [3] ), face-centered cubic (FCC) ( [4] ), and/or hexagonal close-packed solid-solution phases ( [5] ) instead of intermetallic compounds ( [6] ). Moreover, the random distribution of multiple elements with different atomic radii leads to a severely distorted lattice with variations in the interatomic distances along the crystallographic direction of the unit cells ( [3] ). These features, in turn, contribute to desirable mechanical properties, such as high hardness, strength, ductility, and softening resistance at room temperature (RT) and elevated temperatures ( [3] ).

High entropy alloys (HEAs) are a new class of metallic materials composed of multiple principle elements in equal or near-equal atomic proportions [1] , [2] . They have been receiving significant research interest owing to their exceptional mechanical and functional properties; see, e.g., refs [3] – [5] . Among various reported HEAs, the equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi (Cantor alloy) [6] is a popular and important prototype of HEAs based on 3d transition metals. Within a wide range of temperature below its solidus, it usually forms a chemically disordered solid solution in face-centered cubic (fcc) structure at ambient pressure [6] – [9] . A unique mechanical characteristic of the Cantor alloy is an enhanced strength-ductility combination with decreasing temperature, while maintaining outstanding fracture toughness at cryogenic temperatures, which was demonstrated to be closely related to the formation of nano-twins and stacking faults in deformation [7] , [10] – [15] . Furthermore, due to the irreversible pressure-induced phase transition from the fcc to the hexagonal close-packed (hcp) lattice, the presence of the hcp structure was recently observed at ambient conditions [16] – [18] . Abstract The microstructure, temperature-dependent mechanical properties and deformation behaviors of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy (HEA) additively manufactured by selective laser melting (SLM) were investigated. SLM-built HEA had a face-centered cubic (FCC) single-phase random solid solution. In addition, SLM-built HEA was composed of epitaxial growth grains, dislocation network and nano-sized oxides. Room- and high-temperature compression tests confirmed that SLM-built HEA has outstanding mechanical properties in all temperature ranges compared to equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEAs reported up to the present. The excellent mechanical properties of SLM-built HEA were achieved with fine grains, high dislocation density and fine precipitates at low temperatures (25 °C to 600 °C), and by high dislocation density and fine precipitates at high temperatures (700 °C or higher). On the other hand, the deformation microstructure showed that slip and deformation twins are the main deformation mechanisms from 25 °C to 600 °C, and slip and partial recrystallization are the main deformation mechanisms above 700 °C. decision.trend: Early studies on high-entropy alloys used atomistic simulations (as in PMC4976365) to reveal how temperature alters deformation mechanisms such as clustering–ordering transitions and thermo-plastic instabilities. This was followed by experimental investigations (e.g., PMC7229066 and PMC11206460) on as‐fabricated HEAs like equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi and refractory NbTaTiV that measured yield strength and plastic flow over a range of temperatures. Although these studies succeeded in highlighting various temperature‐dependent behaviors and dislocation mechanisms, they largely studied phenomena in isolation.
decision.unsolved: A unified, predictive understanding of the interplay between temperature-activated dislocation dynamics and phase (or short-range order) transitions in the as-fabricated state is still missing. This gap prevents a reliable selection and design of materials with controlled, temperature-sensitive plastic deformation.
decision.lever: Implementing in situ mechanical testing coupled with advanced electron microscopy and complementary atomistic simulations on a prototypical HEA (e.g., equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi) to directly correlate evolving dislocation mechanisms and local ordering transitions with temperature
decision.why: This approach naturally extends the trend—from isolated MD and experimental studies—to an integrated methodology that can validate and refine our understanding of atomic- and mesoscale deformation processes. By doing so, it addresses the unresolved need for a predictive framework linking micro-mechanisms with macroscopic, temperature-dependent plastic behavior, thereby justifying the material candidate choice.
